Toyota Land Cruiser Sat Parked for Five Years. Will It Hit the Crusher or the Road?
21 photos
Photo: Flexiny | YouTube
This 2001 Toyota Land Cruiser spent five long years in a backyard, looking every day closer to the crusher than to running again. With over half a million miles on the clock, it looks like it has long reached the end of the road. But an expert in miracle rescues from backyards, barns and junkyards saw potential in it and tried to rescue it.
This 25-year-old Toyota Land Cruiser J90, officially called the Prado in markets such as Europe, Australia and Japan, underwent its last technical inspection back in 2020. The owner used to drive it on a daily basis. The mileage stands as proof of its loyalty and durability. But one day, the engine just did not start. So he left it parked, planning to fix it one day. But that day never came. Until now.
The SUV has traveled 516,623 miles (831,424.13 kilometers). Has it reached the end of the road, or does it still have life in it? Marcus Peetsalu, an Estonian specializing in mechanical restoration, reviving abandoned cars, and starting long-dead engines, believes in the world-famous Toyota durability.
Parked in the backyard for the past five years, sitting on four flat tires, it is entangled in bushes, and the earth has started to claim it. The legendary green paint that Toyota called Imperial Jade Mica is barely visible under the thick layer of dust and grime it collected over the years, after many more during which it had collected miles. The cabin tells the same story of neglect, as spider webs have conquered it entirely.
Photo: Flexiny | YouTube Marcus airs the tires, hoping they will hold air, and tows it out of its entrapment and onto his trailer, leaving the soil devoid of grass where it was parked back in 2021. Nothing has grown under it. But what is under the hood?
Marcus pops the hood where the 3.0-liter 1LD-FTV engine once used to run. This power plant came as a major upgrade of the J90 generation, introducing Toyota’s D-4D common rail direct injection and variable geometry turbocharger to the 3.0-liter inline-four diesel.
The engine pushes out 161 horsepower (163 metric horsepower) and 253 pound-feet (343 Newton meters) of torque, to make it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 12.1 seconds and reach a top speed of 103 mph (165 kph).
A four-speed torque converter automatic transmission, known for extreme durability, puts the power down through all four corners. However, all these should be in Past Tense, because this high-mileage Toyota has the top speed of the trailer that carries it around.
Photo: Flexiny | YouTube It has been a while since it last ran, and it will need more than just some TLC to run again. A new battery is a good way to start, along with a canister of fresh fuel. Marcus also swapped the old fuel pump with one borrowed from a BMW M57 3.0D, the legendary turbocharged straight-six diesel 24-valve inline-six engine produced from 1998 to 2013.
The starter is not working, but the aftermarket alarm does, so Marcus removes it to get rid of the beep-beep soundtrack while he is trying to stay focused on saving the diesel engine. The engine cranks over, but fuel doesn’t reach the injectors.
When it does start, it dies right out, after pushing out a cloud of dark smoke through the exhaust tailpipe. The alternator pulley is seized, so he hammers it to unlock it. And that is it: the 3.0-liter diesel is alive again after five long years of hibernation.
The resurrection proves that Toyota once built bulletproof cars . Marcus test-drives the 25-year-old Land Cruiser both on and off the road to make sure that everything runs properly, but he can hardly see through the terribly dirty windshield. All the good, old SUV needs right now is a proper bath. And it gets its first in five years.
Photo: Flexiny | YouTube At the end of the transformation process, it doesn't look like it did the day it rolled off the production line of Toyota's Tahara plant in Aichi, Japan. But now that all the dirt and debris are gone and everything works under the hood and inside the cabin, it looks ready to hit the road. Or off-road, for that matter.
He doesn’t reveal future plans for the 2001 Toyota, so he might either sell it or return it to its rightful owner. Even though the Land Cruiser has been on the American market since 1998, Toyota kept the Land Cruiser J90 Prado out of the United States due to strategic market segmentation and overlapping model lineups.
However, over the years, it was imported to the U.S. to serve the adventure seekers in the country. Nowadays, clean, moderate-mileage examples sell for roughly $15,000 on the used car market. In the meantime, the low-mileage, collector-grade units can go well above the $30,000 mark. Yeah, bulletproof reliability is still expensive.

The PrSM, pictured here, is a next-generation, long-range precision-strike missile in the US inventory. (U.S. Army/Darrell Ames)
WASHINGTON — The US arm of Italian rocket maker Avio will build and qualify solid rocket motors for Lockheed Martin’s Extended Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile, paving the way for Avio to become a full-time supplier, the companies announced today.
The strategic cooperation agreement will provide Lockheed a second motor source for PrSM and an additional source of motors on the popular GLMRS round once those motors are fully qualified, Avio USA CEO Jim Syring told Breaking Defense in an interview.
“They’re essentially reserving capacity,” he said. “It’s a win for us and it’s a win for Lockheed.”
Tim Cahill, Lockheed’s president of its missiles and fire control, said in a news release that the agreement “enables us to speed up production of essential capabilities, ensuring our customers maintain their competitive edge against emerging threats.”
Solid rocket motors have historically been a chokepoint for the munitions industry after decades of consolidation left L3Harris and Northrop Grumman as the only two domestic providers. New entrants — such as Anduril, Ursa Major and X-Bow — have entered the market and are currently developing and testing motors, but the qualification process can take years.
Although Avio is a longtime producer of solid rocket motors in Europe, its US-based subsidiary is a relative newcomer. It broke ground on its first American manufacturing plant in September, with the 900,000-square-foot plant in Hurt, Va., scheduled to start building motors in 2029.
Avio’s status as a legacy solid rocket motor maker in Europe will give its American arm several advantages that new entrants lack, Syring said. Like its parent company, Avio USA will make certain components like cases and nozzles in house, meaning that it will not have to rely on an already stressed supply chain.
The company’s manufacturing experience also has benefits for training. One selling point for locating the production plant in southern Virginia was the access to trade workers like mechanics, electricians and welders, Syring said. However, all of those employees will need to undergo specialized training in order to take on the demanding job of making rocket motors.
“We’ll be able to take the people that have that technical discipline and experience and train them to be solid rocket motor manufacturing experts, and what we’ll do is we will take advantage of our parent company in Italy to send them over to Italy for three to four months to train in an actual factory,” he said.
Ahead of production, Avio has already begun putting raw materials like steel on order, with plans to purchase equipment with long lead times — like industrial-size mixers, ovens and x-ray machines — by the end of the year, Syring said.
Beyond its work on GMLRS and PrSM, Avio is also conducting engineering work for building the Mk104 solid rocket motor used for Raytheon’s Standard Missile family. The company is slated to complete its critical design review for that motor in spring 2027, Syring said.

1967 Plymouth GTX Has Mopar's Greatest Engine, Two Broadcast Sheets
20 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
In 1966, Plymouth had two B-body intermediates in showrooms: the Belvedere and the Satellite . The Belvedere was the entry-level version, while the Satellite was a more upscale vehicle with certain restrictions in terms of body styles and powerplants. But that didn't stop the company from creating an even more upscale model.
The brand's third B-body arrived for the 1967 model years as the GTX. It was positioned as the range-topping model. And, much like the Satellite, it was restricted to two-door body styles and V8 engines. However, while the latter came standard with a small-block V8, the GTX was a big-block affair.
The Mopar came standard with Chrysler's massive 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB. It was the corporation's largest V8 at that point and delivered 375 horsepower in its four-barrel configuration. Additionally, customers could opt for the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8, which Chrysler debuted in early 1966. This mill was rated at 425 horsepower.
These remained the only engine choices until 1970, when Plymouth added the six-barrel version of the 440-cubic-inch V8 to the options list. This powerplant sent 390 horsepower to the rear wheels. At the end of the 1971 model year, when Chrysler discontinued its high-compression V8 engines, Plymouth opted to phase off the GTX as a stand-alone model.
Unlike the stripped-down Road Runner, which debuted in 1968, the GTX was a slow seller, mainly because it was notably more expensive. The company delivered 44,178 units between 1967 and 1971, an average of under 9,000 examples per model year.
The two-door hardtop you see here is a first-year GTX, one of over 12,000 units made. However, it has Mopar's mighty 426-cubic-inch Hemi , which found its way into significantly fewer examples. Specifically, only 733 cars were equipped with this mill. It's also a four-speed manual car, which makes it one of only 312 GTXs ordered with this drivetrain combo.
A holy-grail Mopar as far as the powertrain goes, this GTX was lucky enough to evade abuse and found its way into 2026 as a restored classic. It's also a blue-on-blue car (or maybe triple-blue?), which is a somewhat rare color combo. The GTX comes with two original broadcast sheets, a copy of the window sticker, and a detailed report by Mopar expert David Wise.
It's been part of the Cowboy Collectibles collection over the past years and will go under the hammer at Mecum's Kissimmee 2027 auction in January. It will share the stage with a 1969 Hemi Road Runner, a rare 1971 Cuda convertible, a 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona, and a 1970 Plymouth Superbird. It will fetch a six-figure sum.
As of this writing, the most expensive 1967 Plymouth Hemi GTX is a blue convertible that fetched $176,000 in 2025. As for the all-time record, it belongs to a 1971 version that changed hands for a whopping $539,000 in 2026.

2027 Toyota Camry Breaks Cover With Nothing New but the Price, 'Cause Why Fix It if It Ain't Broken?
65 photos
Photo: Toyota
Toyota officially unveiled the 2027 Toyota Camry with zero updates. The only thing that changes about America’s best-selling sedan is the price. The model, a complete carryover, will be $700 more expensive next year, regardless of the trim.
The 2027 Toyota Camry is the 2026 Toyota Camry. The automaker sent out a press release of roughly 1,500 words just to let us know that nothing changes for the new model year. Even the photo gallery from last year has been recycled and uploaded to the new press release about the not-so-new car.
At least, the Japanese are being honest about the carryover. You know what they say: If it ain't broke, don't fix it! So Toyota probably had nothing to fix about the Camry, which is the king of the hill in the sedan segment in the United States, where Toyota sold roughly 316,000 units in 2015. The Toyota Corolla with 248,000 units and the Honda Civic with 238,000 units are struggling to keep up.
Furthermore, the Camry has spent more than 20 consecutive years as America’s best-selling passenger car. So, why mess with success? So here we are, looking at a new model year, which is the old model year. This means that the exterior design, interior layout, technology, and powertrain remain the same.
Photo: Toyota The 2027 Toyota Camry carries over the trims of the 2026 Toyota Camry , so customers will be able to choose between the LE and XLE, focusing on comfort and a comfort-tuned suspension setup, or the SE, Nightshade, and XSE, which feature a sportier appearance and a sport-tuned suspension with unique shock absorbers and springs.
So, the 2027 Camry retains Toyota's signature hammerhead front face with standard LED headlights. As for the cabin, buyers can make choices between the SofTex-trimmed seats on the SE and leather seats featuring "shooting blade" perforations on the XSE.
Lower trims get a 7.0-inch digital instrument cluster and an 8.0-inch touchscreen, while the upper ones (XLE and XSE) come with the dual 12.3-inch display, alongside the 10-inch Head-Up Display. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, a wireless charging pad, and dual-zone climate control are standard across all versions.
The Toyota Camry comes with its proven hybrid-only formula. The 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine with naturally aspirated firepower is paired with either a dual-motor setup for the front-wheel-drive variant or a tri-motor layout for the all-wheel-drive version.
Photo: Toyota The front-wheel-drive Camry gets 225 horsepower (228 metric horsepower) for an acceleration from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.9 seconds and a top speed of 115 mph (185 kph). In the meantime, the all-wheel-drive Camry comes with 232 horsepower (235 metric horsepower), a time of 6.5 seconds from a standstill to 60 mph and an identical top speed.
The 2027 Toyota Camry is scheduled to hit dealerships across the United States later this fall with a price bump of $700 across all trims. This means that the base Camry starts at $29,700. And that is the only new thing about the not-so-new sedan.

Bolt Graphics today announced the completion of the first rounding of testing for Zeus, the GPU it’s designing for HPC, digital twin, and video rendering workloads, as well as the opening of its office in Tawain. While the finished GPU isn’t expected to ship from TSMC until 2028, Bolt is celebrating the test chip being the first commercial GPU architecture with dedicated hardware to execute Maxwell’s equations, complex physics algorithms used for electromagnetic (EM) simulations.
“We’ve proved in this test chip that we can do a highly complex physics algorithm, accelerated in hardware, which no one’s done before,” Bolt Graphics Founder CEO Darwesh Singh tells HPCwire . “There are other chips that do ray tracing in hardware and rasterization. Obviously that’s Nvidia ‘s bread and butter. The EM simulation, the physics stuff, is where there’s a lot of novelty.”
Bolt basically took the entire algorithm that’s implemented in a Cuda kernel and made “a fixed function block in the chip” that runs that kernel,” Singh says. It doesn’t use any of the vector cores or CPU capability in Zeus, and is dedicated to running Maxwell’s equations,which are used to build numerical models of complex, multi-dimensional electromagnetic fields, wave propagation, and material interactions. The algorithms are commonly used in semiconductor design, which is one of the possible use cases that Singh has in mind for the Zeus GPUs.
Zeus PCIe card
EM is Bolt’s starting point for phyiscs modeling, but the company’s goal is to let users “accurately simulate anything in the world by building a complete physics simulation solution,” Singh says. “For years, engineers have had to choose between simulating individual components or building a physical prototype of complete products. Running Maxwell’s equations on our silicon eliminates that tradeoff.”
Singh founded Bolt Graphics in 2020 to develop a low-cost but powerful GPU to run compute-intensive HPC and computer graphics applications. Traditional HPC workloads, such as modeling and simulation, often prefer large amounts of double-precision floating point (FP64) performance, while graphics-intensive workloads, such as ray tracing and rasterization, do well with FP32 and FP16.
Bolt has designed Zeus with powerful vector cores to deliver large amounts of FP64, FP32, and FP16 performance, as well as matrix cores for INT16 and INT8 (not to mention the dedicated block for Maxwell’s equations).
These are traditional workloads for GPUs, but traditional GPUs suppliers have shifted their focus with their latest GPUs to AI workloads, which don’t require the same level of precision as HPC workloads. Nvidia is relying on the Ozaki scheme to emulate FP64 from lower-precision cores, while AMD has bifurcated its GPU lineup with one line designed for AI workloads and its lower-precision cores and another with lots of native FP64 cores to power modeling and simulation on supercomputers.
“We’re hyper focused on these segments,” Singh says of mod/sim, digital twin, and computer graphics. “And so I think our product is going to be better for HPC use cases just because we’re so focused on it.”
Zeus Spec Sheet (Image courtesy Bolt Graphics)
Bolt completed tape-out of Zeus in April and just finished completed the first round of testing of the test chip, a 6 square millimeter chip built using TSMC’s 12 nanometer process. The first round of tests went better than expected. “We’ve exceeded our own performance and power expectations,” Singh says. “It’s better than we thought. So we’re pretty happy actually.”
When Zeus enters production in late 2027 or early 2028, Bolt will use TSMC’s 5 nm process for its 400 square millimeter chip, which is based on a chiplet architecture with an integrated RISC-V CPU. While Nvidia and AMD are utilizing TSMC’s 2nm and 3nm process (N2 and N3) for their GPUs, Bolt purposefully picked TSMC’s 5nm process (N5) to keep costs down and supplies high.
“We don’t need to [use the latest greatest process],” Sing says. “It’s too expensive and it’s hard to get the wafers. We designed the architecture of the chip knowing that we were going to pick N5. It’s not like we tried N3 and found out that it was too expensive and went back. We actually decided on N5 initially and we kept to that.”
That mantra of delivering the most bang for the buck with differentiated silicon while keeping the rest of the stack simple and affordable can be seen throughout Bolt’s design for Zeuss.
For instance, Bolt eschewed high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that AMD and Nvidia use in favor of LPDDR5 memory, which isn’t as fast but offers greater capacity (more than 1TB) than HBM. Bolt also uses plain vanilla Ethernet 400G connectivity for its server- and rack-based solutions, and offers a PCIe-based GPU card for customers that want to upgrade existing systems or build their own machines.
Bolt Graphics plans to deliver 20 teraflops of FP64 with its Zeus 4c offering (Image courtesy Bolt Graphics)
“Those are all things that make it easier for us to scale to millions of units without having to run into major roadblocks, like a competitive supply chain,” he says. “We try to stay away from the exotic stuff, outside of our chip itself. The rest, we want it to be as centered as possible, because it’s too much complexity, too much risk otherwise.”
One of the potential use cases Zeus and its dedicated Maxwell equation cores is doing the EM analysis for optical networking. “EM simulation is important for photonics chips,” Singh says. “You need to run a lot of simulations to find the right geometry of the photonic circuit, the right material, the right distance between the components. And that stuff is currently currently done by intuition.”
Since Zeus could help photonics builder, could that potentially pave the way for integrating the GPU with photonics via co-packaged optics (CPO), as Nvidia and AMD are currently doing? “Not in our first generation,” Singh said. “We are exploring it for a second. It’s just way, way, way too expensive right now.”
Silicon products have soared in cost thanks to the AI boom and the pressure it’s putting on stocks of processors, memory, and storage. Bolt is trying to build a GPU that maximizes the high-end FP64 performance that matters to some customers, while keeping the other costs low. Potential clients including government labs, corporations, and others, Singh says.
“We are in discussions with multiple national labs, defense contractors, hyperscalers, film studios, game studios, you name it,” he says. “On the end user side, all of these segments are very interested in in our differentiated approach to GPUs and GPU systems.”

BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army.
The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.
Travis Langer, BAE Systems’ communication manager, explained to Military Times that the systems together fill a capability gap created by evolving technological threats and the military’s traditional procurement process.
“Both products complement existing air defense systems, but each offer a more cost-effective solution for defense against high-volume, low-cost threats allowing the preservation of high-value missiles for the most critical targets, which extends the life and effectiveness of the entire missile stockpile,” Langer said.
The Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System
According to BAE Systems, MDACS forms the kinetic layer of the defensive shield, using precision-guided munitions called Hypervelocity Projectiles, or HVPs, for both offensive and defensive operations.
“It fills a gap that traditional artillery cannot, providing a scalable layer of protection that complements existing high-tier systems,” Langer said, adding that it allows the Defense Department “to maintain a sustainable defense without draining the budget on every single engagement.”
He explained MDACS combines high-accuracy guidance with the extreme velocity of the HVP. “We reduce the time-to-target and the window the enemy has to maneuver,” he said. “We are collaborating with the Army to integrate the organic sensor network and IBCS to ensure the system remains lethal even when GPS is unavailable.”
Compared with traditional missiles, HVPs are smaller and less expensive, allowing troops to carry tens to hundreds of rounds in a magazine. Rather than relying on a rocket motor, the projectiles use what the company describes as a “low drag aerodynamic design” to achieve high velocities, maneuverability and extended range.
For offensive operations, MDACS will fire the Scorpio-XR, the latest addition to the HVP family. Designed for artillery units, the projectile is expected to double the range of existing 155mm cannon-launched precision munitions, according to the company.
Langer added that MDACs will use HVP rounds to engage air targets, counter-missile and Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System, or C-UAS, while the Scorpio-XR round will be used to defeat fixed and moving ground targets in contested environments.
BAE Systems secured an Army agreement to develop a prototype of MDACS in January 2025, according to reports . The Army had planned to spend approximately $646 million on the project through fiscal year 2027.
The High-Power Microwave
BAE Systems describes its HPM system as a “scalable directed energy weapon” built with an emphasis on affordability. The company said 99% of the system’s components are commercial off-the-shelf parts.
Unlike kinetic weapons, the HPM uses “focused electromagnetic energy” to neutralize airborne threats, specifically “high-volume, low-cost” threats, such as drone swarms, that can strain conventional air defenses.
A video simulation of the system shows the HPM mounted on a trailer in a field. Its sensors automatically detect an approaching swarm of drones, prompting a large magnet to shift into position before the system unleashes what the company describes as “billions of pulses” at the airborne targets.
Although the system remains in the prototype stage, BAE Systems said it has reached Technology Readiness Level 6, or TRL 6. That designation means a technology has been demonstrated in a relevant environment beyond laboratory testing.
Layered air-defense
Langer explained that the two systems are not specifically designed to be used together, but they could complement each other if the mission set requires it.
“MDACS is C-130 transportable, allowing it to deliver rapid, high-rate firepower wherever the fight demands. It is designed to protect critical assets from drone attacks and missile threats, providing a scalable and efficient layer of protection,” he said.
Whereas he called the HPM “an effective layer of wide-area protection” that can complement existing kinetic and missile systems. Langer said it creates “a comprehensive shield for armed forces installations and forward-deployed units.”
As for when soldiers will begin fielding these new systems, Langer said they’re still prototypes. “Final testing and qualification decisions are made by the government,” he concluded.

U.S. Army 2nd Lt. Tiffany D. Jessop, assigned to 4th Squadron, 10th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 4th Infantry Division, operates the ODIN software platform during a division reconnaissance and security experiment as part of Project Convergence Capstone 6 at Fort Irwin, California. (U.S. Army photo by Staff Sgt. Ger’vonni Straun)
WASHINGTON — In just ten days, the Army will activate Project Gatekeeper, a new AI-enhanced cybersecurity sandbox designed to vet commercial software for use on Army networks, officials announced today.
Launching Oct. 23, Project Gatekeeper is creating a single sandboxed environment — running on the Army’s cloud but isolated from operationa l networks and sensitive data — where companies can bring their software for assessment, even if they don’t have an Army contract or a program manager to sponsor them. Officials say Gatekeeper will cut the time required to get software approved fro m months to “minutes” — without sacrificing security in the process.
“Success, to me, looks like a company, within minutes, is able to log in, submit their code and get the green check mark from our pipeline that says you are good to go,” acting Army Chief Information Officer Gabe Chiulli told reporters at the annual AUSA conference here this morning.
Compare that with the current, cumbersome clearance process that can take days or weeks — stalling some software projects for as long as nine months, Chiulli and other officials said. That’s a long time to wait for a software upgrade, especially under a process that officials say lack consistent cybersecurity practices, transparency for contractors and visibility for Army leaders into what’s actually happening on their networks.
“We have had to do a lot of weird janky things to get code into our environments,” Chiulli said. Sometimes, he said, “I’m not sure how they’re getting code over to us.”
The root of the problem, officials said, is that the Army has lacked a single, standardized, centralized process for bringing commercial software onto its secure networks. Instead, “it was up to every program manager,” explained David Markowitz, the service’s chief data and analytics officer.
But many program offices lacked the capability or willingness to conduct cybersecurity assessments of new and unfamiliar code. Rather than evaluate the software themselves, they would wait for another organization to vet the company and officially grant its software Authority To Operate (ATO) on military networks.
“A lot of times, organizations in the Army won’t talk to [companies] until they have this ‘golden ATO,’” Chiulli said.
That created a kind of Catch-22 : The companies best positioned to win Army software contracts where often the ones that already had them. Meanwhile new, innovative entrants — the kind of companies that the Pentagon’s been courting for over a decade — struggled to navigate the combined complexities of cybersecurity rules, procurement regulations and Army bureaucracy.
If a program manager did decide to give a new piece of software a chance, moreover, they rarely had a dedicated, isolated sand box in which t o test it. Instead, they had to bring it onto an Army network and assess it there. That, in turn, required the company’s personnel to get cleared for Common Access Cards (CAC) so they could access the Army system.
“We spent a lot of time and energy trying to get people CAC cards simply to help work with us,” Chiulli said. “This is to get rid of all that [and] lower barriers to entry.”
Gatekeeper will let companies test their software before they have an Army contract, a program manager sponsoring them or even a formal request for proposals to respond to, the officials emphasized, allowing prospective vendors to identify and address cybersecurity problems before trying to do business with the service.
Companies will still need CAC cards to access the platform initially, officials acknowledged. But the Army is finalizing an agreement with the General Services Administration (GSA) to use its Login.gov platform, which allows secure access to government systems for members of the public.
“We’re looking at mid-November to have that integrated, at which point we’ll be able to make this actually commercially accessible,” said David Wright, chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center (ASIC).
Once a company gets access to the Gatekeeper platfor m, it can upload its software and run it through the Army’s standardized cybersecurity tools, including an AI assessment, offi cials explained. In minutes, the automated system will either tell the company its software passed the test or give detailed, actionable feedback explaining why it failed.
Gatekeeper will also include the Army’s DevSecOps software development kit, Wright said, giving companies a secure environment in which to address problems using tools the Army itself has vetted.
“The idea here is not to lessen the security requirements,” Wright emphasized, “but more to make the process more accessible and available, so that they can get immediate feedback and understand what it is that needs to be adjusted or corrected before these things are brought into an Army environment.”

Mercedes-AMG’s GT SUV Is Coming for the Porsche Cayenne Electric - Rendering
8 photos
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik
Mercedes has plenty of things on its plate these days, as it is preparing to update several models. Not only that, but its performance-oriented division based in Affalterbach is also about to expand its portfolio.
You do know what we are talking about, don’t you? That’s right, the upcoming Mercedes- AMG SUV , which does not yet have an official name. Well, it likely does, we just do not know it, as the automaker hasn’t released that many details about it. It is simply known as the GT SUV so far for a very good reason: it builds on the same platform as the all-new GT 4-Door Coupe . You know, the electric model that definitely won’t win any beauty pageants.
That’s quite a surprising move, to say the least, because while most gearheads and their pets can agree that the new-gen Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe is anything but pretty, yet that hasn’t stopped the company from giving it a high-riding alternative. We have seen the upcoming machine on a few occasions, mostly with camouflage wrapped around its entire exterior, but the rendering crowd has also done a great job, for the most part, at imagining what it looks like beneath the fake skin.
It was at the end of last week that we have seen a quite realistic take on it , and that one came from @sugardesign_1 on Instagram. More recently, the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV has been imagined yet again, and the computer generated images that you can see in the photo gallery here came from @kelsonik. This pixel master’s work is usually on the very realistic side of things, so what you see here is basically what you will get when the model finally goes official, and the unveiling date is right around the corner in case you forgot.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik Mercedes itself recently announced that this model is due just shortly. It will be officially shown to the world this week, and the date to save is October 17, 2026. That’s this Saturday, in case you were wondering. Codenamed the X591, the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV looks very similar to its low-riding sibling. It features an almost-identical front fascia, complete with the familiar-looking star-studded headlights, linked together in the middle by a thin light strip.
Further down, it will have a familiar Panamericana grille with vertical slats, decorated in the middle by the three-pointed star logo. The front bumper is home to a pair of vertical vents, and to an air intake on the lower part. Further back, it features similar lines to the new Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe on the sides, as well as flush door handles, but the profile does not have anything else in common with it.
That’s because the doors and side windows are much taller here, to no one’s surprise, and there are also some discreet roof rails on deck. The rear fascia is home to the same quirky lighting signature, as well as the trim surrounding it, and the one in the middle of the tailgate. The rear bumper is an adaptation of the one equipping the GT 4-Door Coupe. The diffuser is a bit less aggressive on this crossover, and the wheels are similar in these renderings signed by the quoted pixel master.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik Mercedes-AMG’s GT SUV is presented here in yellow, and it is contrasted by the black elements. These include the roof, roof rails, side window surrounds, rear diffuser, the outer edges of the roof-mounted spoiler, the grille, and the wheels, among others. The rendering artist has done a great job at sketching out this upcoming model, because as we already told you, the CGI-infused design is realistic.
Look for the same powertrain family as the new Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe, with a tri-motor setup powering the crossover in the range-topping flavor. The low-riding model has 1,153 hp (860 kW/1,169 ps) to play with and 1,475 lb-ft (2,000 Nm) of torque in total in the top-of-the-line grade, taking 2.1 seconds from 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) with the 1-foot rollout, or 2.4 seconds without it. Flat-out, it will do 186 mph (300 kph), and it has a 432-mile (696 km) range with the 106 kWh battery pack fully charged.
We expect similar performance from the upcoming Mercedes-AMG GT SUV , though this model should be a tiny bit slower. A dual-motor setup is likely on the cards, too, offering 805 hp (600 kW/816 ps) and 1,328 pound-feet (1,800 Nm) of torque. Additional highlights will likely include rear-wheel steering, air suspension, semi-active roll stabilization, and a few other things.
With the official unveiling date just a few days away, we do not have to wait that long to learn the secrets of this model, which will take on the likes of the Porsche Cayenne Electric, including its name. But if you held the reins of Mercedes, what would you name the electric super crossover? To be honest, the GT SUV is not a bad name at all, though it’s not exactly the most inspiring either.
